steps.body: You already measured angles in degrees. Now name their parts: an angle forms where two rays share a starting point, called the **vertex.** The two rays themselves are the angle's **sides.** Every angle you measured was really two rays meeting at a vertex.
Open the two rays and read the angle on the protractor. The wider the opening, the larger the degree measure — the rays' length never matters.

widget.prompt: Open the rays to measure exactly 60°.
widget.successFeedback: 60° — an acute angle, two-thirds of a right angle.
widget.lowFeedback: Still narrower than 60°. Swing the ray up to open it wider.
widget.highFeedback: Opened past 60° now. Bring the ray back down to narrow it.

options.label: How far apart the rays have turned

predict.reveal: Angles measure TURN: 60° of opening is 60° whether the rays are stubby or a mile long. Stretching a ray changes the picture, not the angle — the protractor only watches the spread.

cml.actionGoal: Rotate the ray to create the turn and reason about angle size independently of ray length.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If both rays are drawn twice as long, what happens to the angle measure?

options.label: The amount of turn between the rays, not their lengths.
options.feedback: Exactly. Angle measure is invariant under changing ray length.

options.label: Longer rays make a larger angle.
options.feedback: That describes a surface feature, not the mathematical relationship that must remain true. Angle measure is invariant under changing ray length.

widget.prompt: Two rays share a starting point at point B, then spread apart toward points A and C. What is point B called?

options.label: The vertex
options.feedback: The shared starting point of the two rays is always the vertex.

options.label: A side
options.feedback: The SIDES are the two rays themselves (toward A and toward C). B, where they meet, is the vertex.

options.label: A line segment
options.feedback: B is a single point, not a segment with two endpoints. It's the vertex where the two rays meet.

options.label: The degree measure
options.feedback: The degree measure describes the angle's SIZE, not a point. B, where the rays meet, is the vertex.

explanationVariants: The two rays forming the angle are its sides.
Everything except the shared vertex point belongs to the sides.

widget.prompt: An angle is formed by two rays meeting at a vertex. What are the two rays called?

options.label: The sides of the angle
options.feedback: The two rays are the angle's sides.

options.label: Vertices
options.feedback: There's only ONE vertex per angle — the shared point. The rays themselves are called the sides.

options.label: Line segments
options.feedback: Rays have only one endpoint each and extend forever — they aren't segments. They're the angle's sides.

options.label: Degrees
options.feedback: Degrees measure the angle's size, not its rays. The rays themselves are the sides.

steps.body: Angles get precise names using three points: one on each ray, with the **vertex always in the middle.** Angle ABC means a ray toward A, the vertex at B, and a ray toward C. Swap the outer letters and it's still the same angle — but the vertex letter never moves from the middle.

explanationVariants: In angle XYZ, the middle letter Y is always the vertex.
The vertex is whichever letter sits in the middle of the three.

widget.prompt: An angle is named XYZ. Which point is the vertex?

options.label: Y — the middle letter
options.feedback: The vertex is always the middle letter in a three-letter angle name.

options.label: X — the first letter
options.feedback: The first letter names a point on one ray, not the vertex. The vertex is the MIDDLE letter: Y.

options.label: Z — the last letter
options.feedback: The last letter names a point on the other ray. The vertex is the MIDDLE letter: Y.

options.label: All three are vertices
options.feedback: An angle has only ONE vertex. In XYZ, that's the middle letter: Y.

steps.body: Match the angle name to its vertex.

widget.prompt: Match each angle name to its vertex point.

pairErrors.feedback: E is the vertex of angle DEF. For angle MNO, the middle letter — and the vertex — is N.

widget.missFeedback: The vertex is always the middle letter of the three.
widget.successFeedback: PQR's vertex is Q, MNO's is N, DEF's is E — always the middle letter.

explanationVariants: Angle ABC and angle CBA name the same angle — the outer letters can swap, but B stays the vertex in the middle both times.
Only the middle letter's position matters, and it hasn't moved.

widget.prompt: Do angle ABC and angle CBA name the same angle?

options.label: Yes — B is the vertex in both, just the outer letters swapped
options.feedback: The vertex (B) stays in the middle both times — swapping the outer letters doesn't change which angle it is.

options.label: No — different letter orders always mean different angles
options.feedback: The vertex is what matters, and B is in the middle of both names. They name the same angle.

options.label: No — CBA would have C as the vertex
options.feedback: The MIDDLE letter is the vertex in both names — that's B, not C, in CBA. Same angle.

options.label: Can't tell without seeing the rays
options.feedback: The naming rule alone settles it: B is the middle letter in both ABC and CBA, so it's the same angle either way.

hints: The gate's hinge is where the two rays (the gate and the fence) meet.
That shared point is the vertex.
Name the angle using the vertex as the middle letter.
explanationVariants: The hinge is the vertex, so the angle's name must have the hinge's letter in the middle, like GHF where H is the hinge.
Any name works as long as the hinge letter sits in the middle.

widget.prompt: A gate's hinge is at point H. The gate swings between point G (fence) and point F (open gate). Which correctly names this angle?

options.label: Angle GHF — H (the hinge) is in the middle
options.feedback: The hinge H is the vertex, so it must sit in the middle of the angle's name.

options.label: Angle HGF — G is in the middle
options.feedback: That makes G the vertex — but the HINGE (H) is where the rays actually meet. H must be in the middle.

options.label: Angle GFH — F is in the middle
options.feedback: That makes F the vertex — but F is just where the gate swings to, not the hinge. H must be in the middle.

options.label: Any order works equally well
options.feedback: The vertex must be in the middle specifically. Since H is the hinge, it has to be the middle letter: GHF.

takeaways: Two rays sharing a starting point form an angle; that shared point is the vertex.
The rays themselves are the angle's sides.
A three-letter angle name always puts the vertex in the middle.
steps.teaser: next: reading a whole figure full of points, lines, and angles at once.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **The vertex is where two rays meet, and it's always the MIDDLE letter in the angle's name.** For angle RST, the vertex is S — the letter sitting between R and T.

explanationVariants: In angle RST, S is the middle letter — the vertex.
The vertex is whichever letter sits in between the other two.

widget.prompt: An angle is named RST. Which point is the vertex?

options.label: S
options.feedback: S is the middle letter — the vertex.

options.label: R
options.feedback: R is the first letter, a point on one ray. The vertex is the middle letter: S.

options.label: T
options.feedback: T is the last letter, a point on the other ray. The vertex is the middle letter: S.
